correctness.rationale: The unit-ball representation follows from the integral-vertex structure of the truncated cube in each orthant. The dual generating functionals are precisely the coordinate signs and half sign vectors, with the finite norming-pair reduction proved by convex decomposition. For every vertex and every generator, either it norms the vertex (giving a numerical-radius bound v), or the vertex splits into two signed-pair vertices each normed in absolute value by that functional (giving bound 2v). The root vertices form the whole unit ball, so ||T||<=2v. For T(x)=(x1+x2)e3, ||T||=2 and v=1 by exhaustive norming vertex cases, giving equality. Quantifiers cover all real operator matrices and every integer d>=4; no finite experiment is substituted for the all-d proof. Exact standalone finite checker tests d=4,5,6,7.

originality.rationale: The all-dimension exact numerical index of type-D root-polytope spaces was not stated in the closely related primary literature or accessible public records inspected. A general finite-facet reduction is known, but its existence does not compute this new family-specific exact invariant; the essential new ingredients are an explicit two-vertex supporting decomposition and a rank-one equality witness. The equilateral free-space theorem covers the dimension-three A3/D3 case only: any d-dimensional free space over d+1 points has at most d(d+1) molecular extreme points, whereas this type-D unit ball has 2d(d-1), strictly greater for d>=4. No covering statement was found under the tested aliases; priority is only best-knowledge.

value.rationale: The result computes a natural nontrivial operator-theoretic isometry invariant exactly for an entire classical symmetric root-polytope family in every dimension >=4, including the four-dimensional regular 24-cell. It gives both a structural two-root norming decomposition and a sharp explicit rank-one witness. The dimension restriction deliberately excludes a previously covered three-dimensional instance. It is neither an arbitrary coordinate slice nor an exercise about a single small example; the dimension-independent transition and precise constant provide a reusable geometric benchmark.
